cognate: *h1ger- 'wake' in the reduplicated perfect stem *h1ge-h1gor- (Gk ἐγρήγορ-, Ved. jāgṛ-/jāgā́ra, lexicon pie-lex-h1geh1gore) + *swep- 'sleep' (Gk ὕπνος < *sup-no-, Ved. √svap-/svápna-)
drift_or_renewal: Greek keeps *swep- only in the noun (κατ' ὕπνον); the verbal member is renewed by καθεύδω/εὕδω, where Vedic uses the participle of √svap-. Latin renews both members (uigilans / dormio, somnus).
shared_syntax: polar pair of participles: Gk τοῖς ἐγρηγορόσι (pf. ptc.) vs τῷ καθεύδοντι / καθ' ὕπνον; Ved. jāgrataḥ ... svapantaḥ (pres. ptc. of the intensive-perfect stem vs pres. ptc. of √svap-), the two states set against each other as a pair
context: Not fully congruent. In Vedic the pair is a fixed merism in expiation and protection formulas ('whatever sin we did waking or sleeping', 'whoever attacks us sleeping or waking': RV 10.164.3, AV 6.45.3, 6.96.3, 6.115.3, 7.108.3, 8.6.15, a dozen AV/Khila loci). In Aristotle it is an epistemic contrast (dream images false, waking images true; sleeping vs being awake). Aeschylus has the same pair in poetry.
note: The pair is a natural antonym that any language can form, and the Greek witness is philosophical prose with no formulaic use. The point of interest is the matching reduplicated perfect stem on the 'wake' side and the participial form of the pair, not a shared context.

cognate: *ǵʰeim- 'winter/cold' (Gk χειμών/χεῖμα ~ Ved. himá-) exact; the heat member is from *gʷʰer- 'warm' on both sides (Gk θέρος ~ Ved. gharmá-), with ghraṃsá- in AV 13.1 a related or uncertain formation
drift_or_renewal: Greek has the seasonal sense (summer/winter); Vedic has the physical sense (heat/cold), with himá- 'cold, winter' between the two. The heat word differs in formation (θέρος vs gharmá-/ghraṃsá-).
shared_syntax: coordinated or contrasted polar pair: heat-word vs cold-word (Mirab. 114: summer fire against a winter spring of icy water; AV 13.1.96: from him heat, from him cold; RV hiména ... ghraṃsám/gharmám: they warded off the heat with cold)
context: Partly congruent. Both are alternations of heat and cold from one source: a rock that sends out fire in summer and cold water in winter, and Rohita from whom heat and cold are born. The Homeric merism χείματος οὐδὲ θέρευς (Od. 7.118, the garden that bears fruit all year) is the poetic Greek use.
note: Seasonal and heat/cold opposites are among the most generic pairs there are. Of the cognates only *ǵʰeim- is exact; the heat member is a root match only. Kept as a weak lead.

cognate: *mélit- 'honey' + *dl̥kú- 'sweet' (Lat. mel, dulcis ~ Gk μέλι, γλυκύς, with irregular γλ- for *δλ-)
drift_or_renewal: Indic renews both words (mádhu- 'honey' < *médʰu-, which in Greek drifted to μέθυ 'wine'; svādú-/svā́dīyas- < *sweh2dú-, Greek ἡδύς). Homer also has the *sweh2dú- side in ἡδυεπής (Il. 1.248), next to μέλιτος γλυκίων αὐδή in Il. 1.249, matching Vedic svā́dīyo ... vocata.
shared_syntax: Lopsided. In the slab only Plautus has the figure: comparative 'sweet' + ablative of comparison of 'honey' (melle dulci dulcior), which matches Homeric μέλιτος γλυκίων (genitive of comparison) and Vedic mádhunaḥ svā́dīyaḥ / madhor madhutaraḥ (ablative). The Aristotle anchors have only the two cognates side by side in a list (μέλι καὶ ὁ γλυκὺς οἶνος; μέλι καὶ γλεῦκος), not the figure.
context: The supporting witnesses agree in context. Speech sweeter than honey: Il. 1.249, Nestor's voice; RV 8.24.20, speak words sweeter than ghee and honey; AV 3.30.4, madhumatīṃ vācaṃ in the slab's context line. A lover sweeter than honey: Plautus Asin. 614, said to the beloved; AV 1.34, a love charm, 'I am sweeter than honey'.
phrase: 'sweeter than honey' (*dl̥kú-/*sweh2dú- comparative + ablative of *mélit-/*médʰu-), said of speech or of a lover
note: 'Sweeter than honey' is close to universal (Semitic, Egyptian), and Plautus adapts Greek comedy, so the Latin may echo Greek. Low because the slab anchors are weak and the figure is generic. The honeyed-speech theme in Indo-European poetics is something I recall from the literature.

Almost every pivot is Aristotelian prose paired with Cato, Plautus or AV partners on shared common roots, so nearly all bundles are empty. Three low claims. Rejected: heavy/light (guru/laghu vs βαρύ/κοῦφον, non-cognate second member, generic), dogs+wolves (a taxonomic list), heart+liver (anatomy).
